purpose: Human-centered computing history calibration for sanest-approach reasoning, schema discipline, transport economy, security lineage, enterprise integration, and browser/runtime evolution.

questions.answerCore: Syntax is ambiguity control. Naming styles carry semantic roles for humans, parsers, and agents; UTF-8 gives shared text encoding and round-trip integrity across heterogeneous systems.
questions.principle: Make structure obvious enough that humans, parsers, and AI have fewer chances to misunderstand the same thing.

questions.answerCore: A shared schema separates structure from instances so remote payloads can transmit values, references, and deltas rather than repeatedly explaining meaning. Types, keys, constraints, normalization, and indexes reduce ambiguity and repetition.
questions.principle: Why pay to send information the receiver already knows?

questions.answerCore: Canonical representations became richer and more self-describing while delivery became smarter through caching, compression, pagination, chunking, progressive rendering, lazy loading, and deltas.
questions.principle: Spend bandwidth on meaning, but optimize time-to-first-useful-state.

questions.answerCore: Abstractions moved repeated machine complexity into compilers, runtimes, libraries, memory management, and portable toolchains so humans could express intent with less ceremony and lower error burden.
questions.principle: Move complexity downward into the toolchain so humans can think upward in concepts.

questions.answerCore: Different domains need different cognitive models: SQL for data relationships, JavaScript for behavior, CSS for presentation, HTML for structure. Separation of concerns reduces cognitive load and lets layers evolve independently through explicit contracts.
questions.principle: Give each problem domain a syntax shaped around how humans naturally reason about that problem.

questions.answerCore: SQL inherited uppercase terminal/mainframe culture and case-insensitive keywords. Uppercase became a human visual convention that separates language grammar from schema identifiers; camelHump solves readability of multiword identifiers instead.
questions.principle: Different visual shapes can encode different semantic roles.

questions.answerCore: Lowercase is the natural low-friction typing posture. Capitalization should carry semantic meaning rather than impose constant shift/caps friction.
questions.principle: The keyboard should disappear under the hands.

questions.answerCore: camelHump keeps identifiers compact, parser-safe, and human-readable by embedding word boundaries without extra punctuation. In AI-assisted systems, readable identifiers also act as small semantic hints for models and tooling.
questions.principle: Readability is part of the computational interface.

questions.answerCore: TLS standardized and evolved the secure transport model beyond SSL's vendor-originated lineage, tightening cryptographic design and giving the internet a maintainable public standards path while weak legacy mechanisms were retired over time.
questions.principle: Early invention becomes durable infrastructure through standardization, threat-driven hardening, and removal of obsolete assumptions.

questions.answerCore: Enterprise integration moved from vertically controlled proprietary stacks and custom adapters toward shared schema-driven boundary contracts. RSS/XML feeds demonstrated interoperable structured syndication over HTTP; later XML schemas, SOAP/WSDL, REST/JSON, webhooks, queues, event buses, and streaming APIs refined the same contract-first principle.
questions.principle: Remote systems should understand a stable boundary contract, not an entire internal application.

questions.answerCore: As the web shifted from static documents to programmable applications, browser-specific object models became a compatibility problem. Standard DOMs exposed documents as common manipulable object trees, enabling portable scripting, events, dynamic UI, and later coexistence with specialized surfaces such as Canvas and WebGL.
questions.principle: The DOM is a stable human-facing control interface over complex browser internals.
